text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London closed sharply lower following New York where the market was hit by news that Colombia has opened unlimited coffee sales for July to August. This means private exporters and the Colombian National Coffee Growers' Federation are authorized to export all the coffee they can obtain.

Another factor undermining sentiment was a forecast that no damaging cold is in sight for Brazil's coffee areas. However, cold weather this weekend should be watched, private US forecaster Weather Services Corporation said. July lost $75 to close at $2,085 per tonne, while September lost $79 to close at $2,111 per tonne.

Arabica futures in New York ended sharply lower as the market responded negatively to statements out of Colombia announcing the opening of registrations for 'unlimited' amounts. What the market apparently has overlooked is that the amount of fresh coffee available is quite limited.

Colombian Finance Minister Ocampo stressed that 2.5 million bags would be available for shipment but leading exporters in Colombia said there was no way the country would come anywhere close to this figure, and some predicted that Colombia would be lucky to export even half the amount. Exporters accused Finance Minister Ocampo of sending out some wrong signals.

Adding to the industry's woes, exporters said they were still having a hard time finding buyers for about 300,000 60-kg bags of green coffee for shipment in June because the beans had essentially been priced out of the market. July closed 12.65 cents/lb lower at 251.55 cents/lb, while September lost 7.95 cents/lb to close at 225.10 cents/lb.

ICO - Coffee exports for exporting members of the International Coffee Organization rose to 7.018 million 60-kg bags in March 1997, from 6.668 million bags the same month the previous year, the International Coffee Organization said. That brought total exports in October/April 1996/97 up to 50.079 million bags, up 15 per cent from the 43.497 million bags shipped the same period in 1995/96.

It is interesting to note that the increase during October/March 1996/97 was at nearly 16 per cent. Brazil's market share in October/April 1996/97 rose dramatically to 23.18 per cent from 14.59 per cent in 1995/96. By contrast Colombia's market share fell to 13.53 per cent from 15.43 per cent in 1995/96. In spite of the slight decline in the increase rate, shipments are still well ahead of those of last year indicating, that there must have been some increase in pipeline stocks.

BRAZIL - The Cooperativa Regional de Cafeicultores Em Guaxupe Lta, the largest co-operative in Brazil, told Reuters that 1997/98 production should be between 24 to 25 million 60-kg bags, down only slightly from 1996/97, if the coffee areas escape winter frost. This estimate is within earlier expectations, although forecasts from other Brazilian sources put the crop at 20 million bags or below. Recent estimates for the 1996/97 crop range around 27 to 30 million bags.

FRANCE - France imported 598,449 bags of coffee in February 1997, 6 per cent more than was imported the same month the previous year. That brought total imports since the beginning of 1997 up to 1.210 million bags, 10 per cent more than was imported the same period in 1996. Total imports in calendar year 1996 rose by 7 per cent to 6.696 million bags.

Main suppliers of green coffee in January/February 1997 were Uganda (126,900 vs 88,100 bags), Brazil (193,900 vs 126,700 bags) and Colombia (94,500 vs 114,800 bags). The country exported 223,400 bags of coffee in January/February 1997, 33 per cent more than was exported the same period in 1996. Total exports in calendar year 1996 rose by 10 per cent to 1.186 million bags.
SLOVAKIA - Slovakia imported 44,500 bags of coffee in January/February 1997. Green coffee imports reached 29,500 bags, roast and ground 9,600 bags and solubles 5,400 bags.
